# The Things That Take The Time They Take

There is a category of things in the world that cannot be hurried, and I have become fond of them.

Bread is the easiest example. You can buy commercial yeast that speeds things along, add dough conditioners, and turn out a loaf in under two hours. But the loaf that comes from a sourdough starter, fed and watched over days, tastes like something else entirely. The starter is a community of wild yeasts and bacteria negotiating with each other in a jar of flour and water. You cannot tell them to work faster. You can keep them warm and feed them, then wait. The waiting is not a flaw in the process but the process itself. The sourness, the crackle of the crust, and the open, uneven crumb all come from hours in which nothing appears to be happening.

Trees are the same. An oak does not grow because it is pushed. It grows because sunlight, water, and time are available, and it converts them into wood at a pace that has no interest in our schedules. There is a reason we use tree rings as records. Each ring is a year that could not have been skipped. A drought shows up as a thin band, a good season as a fat one. The tree keeps an honest ledger precisely because it cannot cheat on the time.

I think what draws me to these examples is that they resist a habit of thought that has become nearly automatic: the belief that any process can be improved by making it faster. Often that is true. Nobody mourns the days when a letter took six weeks to cross an ocean. But we have taken a good principle and stretched it past where it belongs. We now expect to speed up things whose value lies in their slowness, and we are puzzled when the result feels hollow.

Consider understanding. There is a kind of knowing that comes from reading a summary, and it is useful. I can tell you in one sentence that the French Revolution began in 1789 amid fiscal crisis and social upheaval. But that sentence is to the actual understanding of the Revolution what a photograph of bread is to bread. The real thing comes from sitting with the contradictions: how people who believed in liberty could build a machine of terror, how reasonable reforms curdled, how everyone involved was improvising with incomplete information. That kind of understanding accumulates slowly, through confusion and rereading and the odd moment when two facts you had held separately suddenly connect. You can't download it. You grow it.

Friendship works this way too. You can meet someone and feel an instant spark, and that is lovely, but trust is a different substance. It is built out of small episodes: the time they showed up when it was inconvenient, the time they said something hard and kind, the time they forgot your birthday and you forgave it. No single episode matters much. The accumulation matters enormously. Old friends share a kind of shorthand that cannot be manufactured, because it is made of a thousand forgotten afternoons.

And there is craft. Anyone who has tried to learn a musical instrument knows the peculiar frustration of the plateau. You practice for weeks and feel no better, and then one morning a passage that was impossible is merely difficult. Nothing visible changed overnight. Your hands and mind were reorganizing themselves in the dark, the way a bone knits. Skill is built during the boring repetition, and rest does part of the work as well. Sleep consolidates what practice lays down. Take out the tedium and the rest, and you take out the learning.

I don't want to romanticize slowness into a virtue that applies everywhere. Some slowness is just inefficiency, and some waiting is merely suffering. A person waiting three months for a medical appointment is not being enriched by patience. The distinction I am after is between delay imposed by dysfunction and duration that is intrinsic to the thing. Bread rises slowly because rising is what it is doing. A bureaucratic form that takes six weeks does not have a comparable excuse. Telling the two apart is a useful discipline, and it usually comes down to a simple question: what is happening during the wait? If the answer is "the thing is becoming itself," leave it alone. If the answer is "nothing, it is sitting in a queue," then by all means, fix the queue.

There is also a psychological dimension to this that I find moving. Impatience is, at bottom, a discomfort with not being in control. When something takes its own time, we are reminded that we are not the authors of every outcome. We can set up conditions, but we cannot command results. The gardener plants the seed and waters it, but the seed does the growing. This is humbling, and I suspect the humility is part of why people who garden, bake, or raise children so often report a certain equanimity. They have made a working peace with the fact that some things happen on their own schedule.

It is tempting to think that this peace is a luxury, available only to those with free afternoons. But I suspect it is more a matter of attention than of leisure. You can watch a pot come to a boil with irritation or with interest. The pot takes the same time either way. What changes is whether those minutes are lost or lived. The kettle, the commute, the line at the store, and the slow download are small classrooms in which we practice one of two things: resisting the present or inhabiting it.

I keep returning to the image of the tree ring, because it holds a consoling idea. Every period of your life, including the thin, dry, unproductive years, becomes part of the structure that holds you up. The drought year is not a gap in the record. It is in the record, and the tree is stronger for having survived it. Not every slow or difficult stretch is secretly a gift, and I distrust anyone who says so too glibly. But some are, and we often can't tell which until later.

So here is my modest proposal, offered without any pretense of having mastered it. Find one thing in your life that takes the time it takes. Bake the bread, tend the plant, learn the song, keep the friendship going through the quiet seasons. Let it be slow on purpose. In a world that constantly promises to save you time, it is a small act of faith to spend some of it on something that cannot be rushed, and to trust that what grows there is real.
